θάνατον ἐπιποθεῖ, διὰ τὰς ἀνω τέρω λεχθείσας αἰτίας. Πρὸς δὲ διάνοιαν μυστήρια
λαλεῖ· καὶ περὶ τῶν ἤδη προγεγονότων φιλοσοφεῖ, καὶ πληροφορεῖ τὸ μέλλον.
Τοιαῦται γὰρ ἀεὶ τῶν ἁγίων προφητῶν αἱ ῥήσεις. Ἐπὶ δὲ αὐτῶν τῶν λέ ξεων
γενόμενοι, σαφηνίσωμεν τὴν διάνοιαν, αὐτοῦ ποδηγοῦντος πρὸς τὴν ἑρμηνείαν, τοῦ
καὶ τὸν ἅγιον Ἰὼβ πρὸς τοὺς ἀγῶνας ἐνισχύσαντος. Στίχ. αʹ. Μετὰ τοῦτο ἤνοιξεν
Ἰὼβ τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ. Ὅτι δίκαιος ἀνοίγει τὸ στόμα, οὐχ ἁπλῶς οὑτωσὶ προσήκει
προσέχειν τοῖς λεγομένοις, ἀλλὰ τὰ ἐκ τῶν λόγων ἀναζητεῖν ὠφέλειαν. Μεστὰ γὰρ
ἀεὶ ὠφε λείας τὰ τοιαῦτα ῥήματα τῶν ἁγίων· καὶ ἀνοίγων τὸ στόμα δίκαιος,
κεκρυμμένους δημοσιεύει θησαυ ρούς. ∆ιὸ καὶ τὸ σκεῦος τῆς ἐκλογῆς ὁ Παῦλος ἐπι
στέλλων φησί· Τὸ στόμα μου ἀνέῳγε πρὸς ὑμᾶς, Κορίνθιοι. Καὶ περὶ τοῦ Κυρίου
γέγραπται ὅτι Ἀνοίξας τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ ἐδίδασκε. Καὶ ἁπλῶς ἐκεῖνος μαρτυρεῖται
στόμα ἀνοίγειν, ὁ σιωπῆς μέτρα πρότερον διδαχθείς. Οὐκοῦν καὶ Ἰὼβ ἀνοίγει τὸ
στόμα 17.69 μετὰ τοῦτο· τουτέστι μετὰ τὸ μέγα τρόπαιον, μετ' ἐκεῖνα τὰ πάθη, οὐκ
ἀβασανίστως φθέγγεται περιαλ γῶν τῷ σώματι, τῆς γλώσσης φθανούσης τὸ τῆς φρο
νήσεως ἔνθεσμον, ἀλλὰ σωφρονῶν καὶ ταῖς φωναῖς ὑποδείκνυται. ∆ηλοῖ δὲ καὶ τὴν
γαλήνην τῆς ψυχῆς καὶ τῶν ῥημάτων τὸ ἐμπρεπὲς ἡ τοῦ ἀνοῖξαι τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ
μαρτυρία. ΚΕΦ. ΙΘʹ. Στίχ. αʹ. Ἕως τίνος ἔγκοπον ποιήσετε ψυχήν μου; Ὥσπερ σώματα
βαρέα ἐπιτιθέμενα ζώων σώμα σιν, κάμνειν ποιεῖν τὰ βαστάζοντα· οὕτως εἰσί τι νες
λόγοι βαρεῖς, οὓς ἀκούσας τις κάμνει. Ὡς ὑπὸ βάρους πιεζόμενος, τῆς δυνάμεως τῶν
λόγων τῶν οὐ κακῶς, καὶ χαλεπῶς, ἢ ἐπὶ λοιδορίας εἰρημέ νων ὑπὸ τῶν ἄλλων δύο
μετὰ Βαλδὰδ ἐληλυθότων, οἱονεὶ φορτίου αἴσθησις βαρέος, ὁ Ἰώβ φησι καμὼν τῇ
ψυχῇ ἐφ' οἷς εἰρήκασιν· Ἕως τίνος ἔγκοπον ποιήσετε ψυχήν μου; –Καὶ μετ' ὀλίγον·
Ὁρᾷς ὡς προγέγραπται ὁ Σαυχαίων τύραννος. Τυ ραννικοὶ αὐτοῦ εἰσιν οἱ λόγοι, οὓς
ἀκούσας ὁ Ἰὼβ, λέ γει· Ἕω τίνος ἔγκοπον ποιήσετε τὴν ψυχήν μου; Οὐχ οὕτως
καθικνεῖται ψυχῆς ἀνθρώπου ἄλλο τι, ὡς λόγος σκληρός. Πολλάκις ὑπομείνας τὰς
βασάνους σώματι προσφερομένας, λόγους οὐχ ὑπέμεινεν. Ὁ μέντοιγε τέλειος
ἀθλητὴς, εἰ καὶ κάμνων, ἀλλ' ὑπο μένει τοὺς χαλεποὺς λόγους. Ὕβριν γὰρ
ὑπομένειν μεγάλου ἀνδρός ἐστιν. ∆ιόπερ ἐν τοῖς ἀνδραγαθήμα σιν ἑαυτοῦ ὁ
Ἀπόστολος λέγει· Λοιδορούμενοι εὐλο γοῦμεν, διωκόμενοι ἀνεχόμεθα,
δυσφημούμενοι παρακαλοῦμεν. Ὥσπερ καθάρματα τοῦ κόσμου ἐγενήθημεν, πάντων
περίψημα ἕως ἄρτι. Καὶ μετ' ὀλίγον φησὶν εἶτα, διὰ τὸ, Ἕως τίνος ἔγκοπον ποιή σετε
ψυχήν μου; Ὁρᾷς; Ἰώβ ἐστιν, οὗ καὶ τὸ βιβλίον οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐξαιρέτως περιέχει ἢ τὴν
ἀνδρίαν αὐτοῦ καὶ τὴν ὑπομονήν. Ἀλλ' ὅμως αἰσθάνεται τῶν καμάτων, ὧν κεκμήκει
ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου τοῦ σκλη ροῦ τῶν ἐληλυθότων αὐτὸν ἐπισκοπῆσαι. Στίχ. γʹ. Γνῶτε
μόνον, ὅτι ὁ Κύριος ἐποίησέ με οὕτως. Ἃ βλέπετε περὶ ἐμὲ, μὴ νομίσητε ἄλλοθεν
ἐληλυ θέναι μοι ἢ ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ. Φοβήθητε τοίνυν. Ὁ γὰρ ἐμοὶ ταῦτα ἐπάγων
δύναται καὶ ὑμῖν ἐπαγαγεῖν. Στίχ. γʹ. Καταλαλεῖτέ μου· οὐκ αἰσχυνόμενοί με,
ἐπίκεισθέ μοι. Πολλάκις καὶ καταλαλεῖ τις κακῶς ποιῶν. Ὅτε ἂν δὲ οὐκ
ἀπερυθριάσῃ, εἰς πρόσωπον λέγει ἐκείνῳ, οὐχὶ ἐλέγχων, οὐδὲ τἀληθῆ λέγων, ἀλλ'
ὀνει δίζων καὶ ὑβρίζων. Τοῖς γὰρ ὑπὸ Θεοῦ τιμωρου μένοις ἐπεμβαίνειν οὐ χρὴ,
ἀλλὰ θρηνεῖν καὶ φο βεῖσθαι. Στίχ. δʹ. Ναὶ δὴ ἐπ' ἀληθείας ἐγὼ ἐπλανήθην, παρ' ἐμοὶ
δὲ αὐλίζεται πλάνος· λαλῆσαι ῥῆμα, ὃ οὐκ ἔδει. Εἶτά φησιν καθ' ὑπόθεσιν· Ὑμῖν
δίδωμι, ὡς ὑπο 17.72 λαμβάνεται, ὅτι διὰ τὰ ἁμαρτήματα ταῦτα πάσχω· ἆρ' οὖν
ἐχρῆν ὑμᾶς οὕτω μοι ὀνειδίζειν; Παρ' ἐμοὶ δὲ αὐλίζεται πλάνος. Εἰ καὶ καθ' ὑπόθεσιν
τοιαῦτα ἐπεποιήκειν, οἷα οὐκ ἔδει· εἰ καὶ τοιοῦτος ἤμην, ἆρ' οὐκ ἐχρῆν ὑμᾶς
βλέποντας μάστιγας, τοὺς ἰχῶ ρας, τοὺς σκώληκας, τὴν ἀπώλειαν τῶν ὑπαρχόντων,
αἰδεσθῆναι; Ἀλλὰ προσεπιβαίνετέ μοι μὴ ἐλεοῦντές με, μηδὲ συμπαθοῦντές μου τῇ
περιστάσει. Στίχ. εʹ. Ἔα δὲ, ὅτι ἐπ' ἐμοὶ μεγαλύνεσθε, ἐνάλλεσθε δέ μοι ὀνείδει. Οὐ
μετρίως μοι ὀνειδίζετε, ἀλλ' ἐναλλόμενοι ὡσπερεὶ ἐπιβαίνοντες καὶ καταπατοῦντές
με ὀνει δίζετε. Στίχ. ʹ. Ὀχύρωμα δὲ αὐτοῦ ἐπ' ἐμὲ ὕψωσεν. Οἱονεὶ ὑπὸ τεῖχος τῆς
περιστάσεώς εἰμι ὀχύρωμα, ὃ οὐ δύναμαι φεύγειν, ἕως οὗ κρινεῖ ὁ Θεὸς καθελεῖν
αὐτό. Στίχ. ζʹ. Ἰδοὺ γελῶ ὀνείδει, καὶ οὐ λαλήσω. Τοῦτό ἐστι τό· Νίκα ἐν τῷ ἀγαθῷ τὸ
κακόν. Τοῦ αὐτοῦ. Ἰδοὺ ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνείδει ὑμῶν γελᾷν, οὐ λαλεῖν νομίζομαι. ΚΕΦ. Κʹ.
pass_a_gloss: ...he longs for death, because of the causes said above. But toward the understanding he speaks mysteries; and about the things already happened before he philosophizes, and gives full assurance of what is going to be. For such are always the sayings of the holy prophets. And having come upon the words themselves, let us make clear the meaning, he guiding the feet toward the interpretation, he who also strengthened holy Job toward the contests. Verse 1. After this Job opened his mouth. That a righteous man opens the mouth: it is not fitting simply, just so, to pay attention to the things said, but to seek out the benefit from the words. For always full of benefit are such sayings of the saints; and opening the mouth a righteous man makes public hidden treasures. Therefore also the vessel of election, Paul, writing a letter says: My mouth has opened toward you, Corinthians. And about the Lord it has been written that Having opened his mouth he was teaching. And simply that one is witnessed to open a mouth who was first taught the measures of silence. Therefore Job too opens the mouth after this; that is, after the great trophy, after those sufferings, he does not utter untested things, being in great pain in the body, the tongue getting ahead of the lawfulness of prudence, but being self-controlled he is shown also in his voices. And the testimony of the 'to open his mouth' shows both the calm of the soul and the fittingness of the words. Chapter 19, verse 1 (KJV 19:2). Until when will you make my soul toil-worn? As heavy bodies placed upon bodies of animals make the ones carrying weary, so there are some heavy words, having heard which one grows weary. As though pressed under a weight, of the power of the words spoken not badly (read: not well), and harshly, or for abuse by the other two who had come with Baldad, as it were the perception of a heavy load, Job says, wearied in the soul at the things they have said: Until when will you make my soul toil-worn? And after a little: You see how the tyrant of the Sauchaeans was written beforehand. Tyrannical are his words, having heard which Job says: Until when will you make my soul toil-worn? Nothing else so reaches down to a soul of a man as a hard word. Often having endured the tortures brought to the body, he did not endure words. The perfect athlete however, even if wearying, yet endures the harsh words. For to endure insult is of a great man. Wherefore in his own brave deeds the Apostle says: Being reviled we bless, being persecuted we hold out, being defamed we exhort. As refuse of the world we became, offscouring of all until now. And after a little he says then, because of the 'Until when will you make my soul toil-worn?': You see? It is Job, whose book also contains nothing else especially than his courage and the endurance. But nevertheless he perceives the toils which he had toiled from the hard word of those who had come to visit him. Verse 3. Know only that the Lord made me thus. The things you see about me, do not think them to have come to me from elsewhere than from God. Fear, then. For the one bringing these things on me is able to bring them also on you. Verse 3. You speak against me; not being ashamed of me, you press upon me. Often someone also speaks against, doing badly. But when he does not stop blushing (read: does not blush), he says to the face of that one, not refuting, nor saying the true things, but reproaching and insulting. For it is not needful to trample upon those being punished by God, but to lament and to fear. Verse 4. Yes indeed in truth I was led astray, and with me lodges a deceiver; to speak a word which was not needful. Then he says by hypothesis: I give to you, as is supposed, that because of the sins I suffer these things; was it then needful for you so to reproach me? And with me lodges a deceiver. Even if by hypothesis I had done such things as were not needful; even if I was such, was it not needful for you, seeing scourges, the ichors, the worms, the loss of the belongings, to feel respect? But you step upon me further, not pitying me, nor suffering with me in my circumstance. Verse 5. But let it be that you are magnified against me, and you leap at me with reproach. Not moderately do you reproach me, but leaping on, as it were stepping upon and trampling down me, you reproach. Verse 6. And his stronghold he raised against me. As if under a wall of the circumstance I am, a stronghold, which I cannot flee, until God judges to take it down. Verse 7. Behold I laugh at reproach, and I will not speak. This is the: Conquer in the good the evil. Of the same. Behold at your reproach I am thought to laugh, not to speak. Chapter 20 (bare label; the note on Job 20:6 follows in u02-open).
pass_b_english: … longs for death, for the reasons stated above. But as to the inner sense he speaks mysteries: he reflects on things that have already happened and gives full assurance about what is to come. Such are always the sayings of the holy prophets. Now that we have come to the words themselves, let us make their sense clear, with him guiding our steps toward the interpretation who also strengthened holy Job for his contests.

“After this Job opened his mouth” (Job 3:1). Since it is a righteous man who opens his mouth, it is not fitting to attend to what is said just casually; we should search out the benefit that comes from the words. For such sayings of the saints are always full of benefit, and when a righteous man opens his mouth, he brings hidden treasures out into public. That is why Paul too, the chosen vessel, says in his letter: “My mouth is open to you, Corinthians” (2 Corinthians 6:11). And of the Lord it is written: “Opening his mouth, he taught” (Matthew 5:2). In short, the one who is attested as opening his mouth is the one who has first been taught the measures of silence. So Job too opens his mouth “after this”: that is, after the great trophy, after those sufferings. He does not speak without weighing his words, in anguish of body, with his tongue running ahead of the lawful rule of good sense; rather, even in his words he shows himself self-controlled. And the testimony that he “opened his mouth” shows both the calm of his soul and the fitness of his words.

“How long will you make my soul weary?” (Job 19:2). Just as heavy loads laid on the bodies of animals make the beasts that carry them weary, so there are some heavy words, and whoever hears them grows weary. As if pressed down by a weight — the force of the words spoken not [well], but harshly or in abuse, by the other two who had come with Baldad, like the feeling of a heavy load — Job, weary in soul at what they had said, says: “How long will you make my soul weary?”

And a little later: You see how the sovereign of the Sauchaeans was described beforehand. His words are tyrannical, and when Job hears them he says: “How long will you make my soul weary?” Nothing reaches a man's soul as a hard word does. Often someone who has endured tortures applied to his body has not endured words. The perfect athlete, though, even when he is weary, still endures harsh words; for to endure insult belongs to a great man. That is why the Apostle, among his own deeds of courage, says: “Being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we bear it; being slandered, we entreat. We have become like the refuse of the world, the scum of all things, until now” (1 Corinthians 4:12-13).

And a little later, on the words “How long will you make my soul weary?”, he says next: Do you see? It is Job, whose book contains nothing so especially as his courage and his endurance. And yet he feels the weariness he had suffered from the hard word of those who had come to visit him.

“Only know that the Lord has done this to me” (Job 19:3). What you see in my case, do not think it has come to me from anywhere but from God. Be afraid, then; for he who brings these things on me can bring them on you as well. “You speak against me; without shame before me you press upon me” (Job 19:3). Often a person even speaks against another and does wrong in it. But when he feels no shame, he says it to the other man's face, not to correct him or to tell the truth, but to reproach and insult him. For one must not trample on those who are being punished by God, but lament and be afraid.

“Yes, truly I have gone astray, and a deceiver lodges with me, so that I speak a word I ought not” (Job 19:4). Then he speaks by way of supposition: I grant you, as you assume, that I suffer these things because of my sins; ought you then to reproach me like this? “And a deceiver lodges with me.” Even if, for argument's sake, I had done such things as I ought not, even if I was that kind of man, ought you not, seeing the scourges, the running sores, the worms, the loss of my possessions, to have felt some respect? Instead you trample on me further, with no pity for me and no sympathy for my plight.

“But let it be that you magnify yourselves against me and leap on me with reproach” (Job 19:5). You reproach me beyond measure; you leap on me, as if stepping on me and trampling me down, as you reproach me. “And he has raised his stronghold against me” (Job 19:6). It is as if I am under a wall: the stronghold of my plight, which I cannot escape until God decides to pull it down. “Behold, I laugh at reproach, and I will not speak” (Job 19:7). This is the saying: “Overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21).
From the same: Look, at your reproach I am thought to laugh, not to speak.
